A.why: F27: an item expected to be realised/settled within twelve months is current.

B.why: Not in the operating cycle and realised after more than twelve months fails every F27 current criterion, so it is non-current.

C.why: F27 makes a liability current when the entity does NOT have an unconditional right to defer settlement for 12 months; having that right makes it non-current.

D.why: F27: cash and cash equivalent is current.

items.missing_decisive_condition: Options A and D are both current under F27; the stem asks 'which' with no 'only'/'except' discriminator, so two options are correct.
items.syllabus_fit: Fair chapter topic (current/non-current), but the item is defective.
items.quality_note: Two correct options (A and D); not usable as single-answer MCQ.
items.source_explanation: Per F27 an item is current if it is expected to be realised within twelve months or is cash and cash equivalent, so both A and D are current. B is non-current (no current criterion met). C is non-current because an unconditional right to defer settlement for 12 months is what makes a liability non-current under F27. With two correct options there is no single answer.

A.why: F25: payment of interest is a charge on profits and is to be paid even if there is no profit.

B.why: F25: dividend, not interest, is an appropriation of profits.

C.why: F25: the rate of interest on debentures is prefixed, not varying with profits.

D.why: F25: debentureholders do not normally have voting rights and interest does not depend on them.

items.quality_note: Clear; distractors plausible and each contradicted by F25.
items.source_explanation: F25 states interest on debentures is a charge on profits payable even if there is no profit, so A is right. B reverses it (appropriation applies to dividend). C is wrong since the debenture rate is prefixed. D is wrong because interest is unrelated to voting rights, which debentureholders normally lack.

items.source_explanation: Following F8's method, normal profit is 30,000, super profit 15,000, and goodwill = 15,000 x 100/10 = Rs. 1,50,000 (D). A is the super profit, C the normal profit, and B capitalises total average profit.

B.why: Shortfall is 5,000, not 20,000 (20,000 is the required capital).

items.numeric_check: C's share 1/4; remaining 3/4 split 2:1: A = 1/2, B = 1/4. Total capital 80,000 (check: 45,000+15,000+20,000 = 80,000). B required = 80,000 x 1/4 = 20,000; existing 15,000; bring in 5,000. (A required 40,000, holds 45,000, withdraws 5,000; C 20,000 matches.)
items.syllabus_fit: Fair, Admission of a Partner (capital adjustment per F10).
items.source_explanation: New ratio is A 2/4, B 1/4, C 1/4, and F10 says capitals are set proportionate to profit share on the total capital 80,000. B's required capital is 20,000 against 15,000, so B brings in Rs. 5,000 (C). A is the withdrawal direction (that applies to A), B uses the whole required capital, and D ignores the deficiency.

A.why: F18: on dissolution of partnership the business is not terminated; closing business and books describes dissolution of firm.

B.why: F18: assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn.

C.why: F18: court does not intervene as partnership is dissolved by mutual agreement.

D.why: F18: economic relationship continues in a changed form; it ends only on dissolution of firm.

items.syllabus_fit: Fair, Dissolution of partnership vs firm.
items.quality_note: Good; distractors are the dissolution-of-firm column.
items.source_explanation: Mutual-consent change of ratio with continuing business is dissolution of partnership, where per F18 assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn (B). A, C and D are the dissolution-of-firm attributes (business closed, court order, relationship ends).

items.source_explanation: R's share is 1/6 of 1,50,000 = 25,000, 5,000 short of the 30,000 guarantee. Per F3 the guaranteeing partners bear the shortfall, here 3:2, so P bears 3,000 and gets 75,000 - 3,000 = Rs. 72,000 (A). B ignores the shortfall; C and D mis-split it.
